title: Learning cornet in Algiers and from local teachers
summary: Love recounts practicing with Vinson and Tom, playing dances at the yard, taking lessons from many local musicians, and his father's advice and insistence he stay home.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Right across the street is the little double house back in the yard. That's where Eddie used to live. Eddie Vinson and Tom Alvin on one side. Oh I see. And I used to go down there and join them every day. They had the bass violin player they called Teep. And when I first come down there I could play the bass. I was a little bit of a fellow. But Tom wanted the cornet playing. He said, get your cornet. We'll all show you. And Eddie Vinson played a vowel trombone you know. And he drilled me through what we were going to play. And then lieutenants would yell at us over in the yard. They didn't have but one building there. And I waked on that building. I was waking. Nothing but a kid. So they used to hear us practicing over there so they hired us one Saturday night to give a dance out there. And we played such good music. So they gave us three nights. Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. And I got busy on the horn and I was taking lessons from everybody. I used to go around to old man Allen's house. Son wasn't born then. And I used to go around. George Hooker used to play cornet in the band. I'd get George to teach me what he knew. I'd go around the baritone players house. George Simms. He would teach me using fine musicians. And every time Charlie the Virgis they called me. Oh yes. Fess I think took lessons from him too. Yeah. And Pete. And me too. I went around and got some of them lessons. Play for nothing. All I want to do is to blow the horn and play. Man I got good. Then me and Tom come into playing down in the platinum parry where all them mosquitoes at. I got good you know and I wanted my pa and them to hear me at home. He said I wasn't going to play no cornet you know. I was a little bit of boy because I wouldn't play soft. I used to play too loud you know. So he told me, he said I ain't the way to study music. Learn how to get a tone and play soft. If you play soft you can play loud when you want. Well that's the fact. So I was playing pretty fair. I wasn't playing all that good when I went home. But he thought it was great. And he said that's my boy. That's son my boy. I went up there with Frankie Duesen and Peter. Joe Oliver on the cornet. Joe Oliver. They had a dance at my home at the Artfellas. I went up there and wake all day with them fellas for nothing. I wasn't getting paid. I just wanted to play with them. Just wanted to learn. My pa was proud of me too. He wouldn't let me come back down there. I had to stay home. Really? Yeah he went and got him a trombone and said you're going to play cornet now. And we had a little band at home they called Love's
